hints: Follow the blood in order - it leaves the heart deoxygenated first, then goes pump to oxygenator to heater, then must return to the heart. Which chamber and which vessel are named in the text?
walkthrough:
Track the One-Way Loop**
Blood is taken from the right atrium because that holds deoxygenated blood returning from the body. That is why your first cannula line must start at the right side of the heart and go into the top arrow leading to the artificial pump.

Return Warmed Oxygenated Blood**
Inside the machine blood goes pump -> oxygenator -> heater in that fixed order. After the heater it is oxygenated and warm, so your second line must go from the bottom arrow back to the vena cava to re-enter the heart circulation.
Final answer: Draw one line from the right atrium to the arrow entering the artificial pump and a second line from the arrow leaving the heater back to the vena cava (superior or inferior).

hints: In the lungs, blood is separated from air by a very thin wall only one cell thick - think where oxygen actually enters the capillary.
walkthrough:
Match Function to Structure**
The oxygenator membrane lets gases through but keeps blood and air separate. In the lung the same job is done by the wall between the alveolar air space and the capillary blood.

Name It Precisely**
That wall is the alveolar epithelium, made of thin squamous cells, plus the capillary endothelium very close to it. The name needed here is alveolar wall / alveolar epithelium.
Final answer: Alveolar wall / alveolar epithelium (wall of alveolus).

hints: Start with which gas is high on each side - oxygen is high in the enriched air, carbon dioxide is high in the venous blood.
Recall how gases cross any exchange surface and why flowing in opposite directions keeps that process fast along the whole membrane.
Link to the normal alveolus features for fast exchange - think distance and area - and apply them to the artificial membrane.
walkthrough:
Set the Gradients**
Oxygen-enriched air has a high partial pressure of oxygen and low carbon dioxide. Incoming venous blood is the opposite - low oxygen, high carbon dioxide. So oxygen moves into blood and carbon dioxide moves out into the air stream.

Explain the Mechanism**
Both move by diffusion down their concentration gradients through the partially permeable membrane. Because blood and air flow in opposite directions, fresh high-oxygen air always meets blood that is already partly oxygenated, and vice versa. This countercurrent arrangement keeps the gradient steep along the whole length so equilibrium is never reached.

Add Fick's Law Features**
Like an alveolus, the membrane is very thin, giving a short diffusion pathway, and provides a large surface area. Both increase the rate of diffusion, allowing the oxygenator to replace lung function.

Final answer: Oxygen diffuses from oxygen-enriched air into blood and carbon dioxide diffuses from blood into air, down their concentration gradients; opposite (countercurrent) flow maintains a steep gradient so equilibrium is not reached; short diffusion pathway across membrane and large surface area give rapid exchange.

hints: Compare the tunica media tissues - the aorta is an elastic artery close to the heart, while a muscular artery further away needs more muscle to control distribution.
Think what hits the aorta first at ventricular systole - a surge of blood at very high pressure that would burst a rigid tube.
Connect stretch then recoil to what happens to pressure and flow during diastole when the heart is not pushing.
walkthrough:
State the Structural Difference**
In Fig. 5.2 the tunica media of the aorta is very thick but dominated by elastic tissue. Compared with a muscular artery, it contains much more elastin / elastic fibres and relatively less smooth muscle.

Stretch Under Pressure**
When the left ventricle contracts in systole it ejects blood at very high pressure directly into the aorta. Elastic fibres allow the wall to stretch, so the aorta expands without bursting and stores elastic strain energy.

Recoil to Smooth Flow**
When the ventricle relaxes, the stretched wall recoils. That squeeze pushes on the blood, maintaining high pressure and evening out the pulsatile flow into a more continuous flow to the rest of the body.

Final answer: Aorta tunica media has more elastin / elastic fibres and less smooth muscle than a muscular artery; this allows the aorta to stretch during ventricular systole to withstand high pressure, then recoil to maintain high pressure and even out blood flow.

hints: Most carbon dioxide is carried not as gas but converted inside red blood cells - what enzyme speeds up that reversible reaction with water?
walkthrough:
Link Observation to Reaction**
You are told most carbon dioxide is converted to hydrogencarbonate ions inside red blood cells. That reaction is $CO_2 + H_2O \rightleftharpoons H_2CO_3 \rightleftharpoons H^+ + HCO_3^-$.

Why the Enzyme Is Essential**
Without catalysis this reaction is too slow for the time blood spends in tissues. Carbonic anhydrase inside the red cell speeds it up, so rapid loading of carbon dioxide as hydrogencarbonate is possible.
Final answer: Carbonic anhydrase catalyses / speeds up conversion of carbon dioxide and water to carbonic acid / hydrogencarbonate ions in red blood cells.

hints: Remember why humans need chloride ions to enter - hydrogencarbonate normally leaves the cell, taking negative charge with it. What happens if it never leaves?
walkthrough:
Recall the Normal Chloride Shift**
In humans, $HCO_3^-$ diffuses out of the red cell into plasma, leaving excess positive charge inside. $Cl^-$ moves in to balance charge - that is the chloride shift.

Apply the Caiman Difference**
Here $HCO_3^-$ combines with haemoglobin and stays inside until the lungs. Because negative ions do not leave, no electrical imbalance develops, so inward movement of chloride ions is unnecessary.

Final answer: Hydrogencarbonate ions remain inside the red blood cells (bound to haemoglobin), so there is no loss of negative charge and no charge imbalance to correct, so chloride shift is not needed.
